At the heart of agile ways of working lies the principle of team autonomy and self-organization. The belief is that autonomous groups and individuals experience greater ownership and engagement, empowering them to solve problems more effectively and innovatively. This is expected to enhance trust and collaboration among team members as well as with customers ( Beck et al., 2001 ; Conboy, 2009 ), ultimately increasing productivity and customer satisfaction through adaptation to changing needs (e.g., Ramasubbu and Bardhan, 2021 ; Schwaber and Sutherland, 2013 ). While this assumption can be challenged in various ways, it has become a key driver for experimenting with organizational structures and new leadership approaches aligned with agile values. Agile is applied through a broad range of frameworks, such as Scrum, XP, and others. Despite appearing simple on paper, these frameworks often encounter complex challenges in real-world implementation, particularly due to the concept of self-management ( Masood et al., 2020 ; Moe et al., 2012 ). When decision-making power is transferred to teams, it becomes clear that this does not imply that individuals or teams can act without constraints. Successful self-management requires a clear and shared purpose, guiding principles, and feedback mechanisms to ensure alignment with the organization's vision and values. Autonomy also requires a delicate balance between freedom and responsibility, as teams must be accountable for their outcomes and transparent about their progress. While this approach may work well in small-scale implementations, the trend toward organizational agility has emphasized the need for this balance. This challenge is evident in the increasing number of frameworks developed to manage large-scale agile implementations, such as LeSS and SAFe, which introduce structures to support governance and control at the organizational level while simultaneously influencing team autonomy ( Gustavsson et al., 2022 ). This other section from the article explores the tension between autonomy and control within self-managing teams in agile project management, highlighting their significance in human experience and societal organization.

In dealing with self-organized teams, our research confronts two oppositions: autonomy and control. These concepts represent two core aspects of human experience, societal organization, and indeed also agile project management. Autonomy, defined as the capacity for self-governance and independent decision-making ( Ryan and Deci, 2000 ), underpins individual freedom, while control refers to mechanisms that guide or constrain behavior. Their relationship is complex and varies across disciplines. In psychology, autonomy involves a sense of choice, whereas control refers to internal or external influences on behavior ( Deci and Ryan, 1987 ). Autonomy supports well-being and motivation, while control can be detrimental, depending on the context ( Deci and Ryan, 1987 ; Gong and Wang, 2023 ). In engineering, these concepts are seen as complementary, enhancing system efficiency and safety (e.g., Martins et al., 2020 ). Sociology often views them in tension, reflecting conflicts between agency and structure, but also as opportunities for empowerment and collaboration (e.g., Steckermeier, 2021 ). Also, disciplines such as law, neuroscience, and AI engage with autonomy and control, each offering different perspectives: law emphasizes external regulation and accountability; neuroscience focuses on self-regulation and neural mechanisms of restraint; and AI examines the balance between human oversight and machine independence. Despite these differences, all address how boundaries between autonomous action and external control are negotiated.

This subsection from the article discusses the definitions of paradox, autonomy, and control within organizational contexts, emphasizing the historical roots of paradox studies in both Eastern and Western philosophical traditions.

Below, we will therefore briefly outline the territories of each of the three concepts in order to understand how they are defined in an organizational context: paradox, autonomy, and control. ### The paradoxes approach

The study of paradoxes has a long history, drawing on both Eastern philosophical traditions such as Taoism and Western philosophy dating back to ancient Greece ( Smith et al., 2017 ). Without engaging in a detailed historical review, this illustrates that paradoxes and contradictions have always attracted attention and represented fundamental challenges in human thought. That said, paradox is a broad concept, and paradoxes come in many forms and types. For example, Smith and Lewis (2011) identified four types of paradoxes: performing, learning, organizing, and belonging. The typology helps us understand how different paradoxes affect different parts of our life, but as most paradoxes overlap these categories, the value of this typology lies in helping us see the widely varying ways that paradoxes affect our world and our lives ( Smith and Lewis, 2011 ). A further source of complexity in paradox theory concerns whether paradoxes are latent or salient. Gaim et al. (2022) state that there is a general consensus around the idea that tensions inherent to organizing are persistent but that their saliency or visibility is situational. Diversity arises in what triggers this saliency. Some scholars emphasize exogenous factors such as environmental conditions of change and resource scarcity ( Smith and Lewis, 2011 ), while others focus on the presence of particular mindsets and cognitive frames ( Miron-Spektor et al., 2018 ; Smith and Tushman, 2005 ). Others highlight endogenous factors such as leadership decisions ( Knight and Paroutis, 2017 ), while still others ( Tuckermann, 2019 ) focus on processes through which contradictions are continuously made visible and invisible, enabling organized action. A central point to be aware of is that paradoxes might be latent for some while salient for others across a hierarchy ( Gaim et al., 2022 ).

Accordingly, our analysis will pay attention both to the paradoxes we identify and to the practices, processes, and problem-solving approaches that surround them. ### Autonomy as challenge in organizational and project research

As already mentioned, the research into organizational autonomy is a less well-defined and less well-developed field. Autonomy as such is a broad and discipline-spanning topic that refers to the ability of an entity to act independently and to self-determine its goals and how to pursue them. In organizational research, it is a fundamental concept that refers to the degree of freedom that an organization or its members have over various aspects of their work, such as decision-making, resource allocation, goal setting, and performance evaluation. Autonomy can be studied at different levels, such as the individual, team, or organizational level. Arregle et al. Here, the question of the different levels, from individual, team, multi-team to organizational context, represents an important focus for research. ### Control as central element in management

Control has, in comparison to autonomy, long been seen as a fundamental and integrated part of organizations. Historically, definitions of organizational control have focused on the manager as the primary developer and implementer ( Cardinal et al., 2010 ), and the study of control has been seen as a study of the mechanisms that can be used to achieve organizational objectives ( Harris et al., 2009 ). The resulting research in formal controls, rooted in principal–agent theory, addresses risks of information asymmetry and opportunism that emerge when ownership and execution are separated ( Eisenhardt, 1985 ; Jensen and Meckling, 1979 ). To mitigate these risks, organizations use monitoring, incentives, and contracts. In projects, this dynamic often occurs between managers and teams or project owners and project members, with traditional controls relying on detailed plans, contracts, and extensive supervision. This is also reflected in project studies, where one can find a focus on formalized and structural control mechanisms. Most likely as a response to uncertainty and complexity around projects, for example, Korhonen et al. (2014) showed how comprehensive control packages help managers cope with uncertainty in project portfolios, while Liu, Borman, and Gao (2014) analyzed how control mechanisms coordinate work and manage system boundaries in complex engineering projects. Other research highlights practice-oriented and contextualized approaches, such as Jünge et al. (2019) , who analyze how control unfolds in projects, where lean project planning and control practices are tailored to the situated context.

This subsection from the article explores the interplay between individual autonomy and personal preferences within agile methodologies, highlighting how prescribed team-level autonomy influences empowerment and motivation.

Delving into the data highlights three main areas of this paradox, which we will present here: individual autonomy and personal preferences, control issues, and roles and tools. ### Individual autonomy and personal preferences

As noted in the introduction, high individual autonomy is empowering and motivating. Even though the agile method prescribes autonomy at the team level, it is found that the individual agile developer is empowered at a higher level than the non-agile developer, even though the difference is not significant ( Tessem, 2014 ). However, agile work practices emphasize team autonomy, which sometimes clashes with the autonomy of individual team members. For example, Moe et al. (2009) note that “In all the teams we studied, implementing shared leadership was troublesome because the team members did not change their individual, decentralized decision-making process” (p. 23). In line with this, both Hoda and Murugesan (2016) and Magpili and Pazos (2018) emphasize individual autonomy as a barrier to team autonomy. The literature highlights the difficulty of incorporating both individual autonomy and team autonomy in the same work environment, noting that “self-managing groups may end up controlling group members more rigidly than they do under traditional management styles” ( Moe et al., 2010 , p. 486). Likewise, Kakar (2018) demonstrated that individual autonomy has a negative impact on team cohesion.

This discussion section from the article explores the discrepancies between formal agile structures and the lived practices of teams, highlighting the importance of shared goals for project success in scaled agile environments.

Also, articles dealing with scaled agile stress the importance of shared goals and visions between teams as well as between the teams and the organization for success of the projects ( Verwijs and Russo, 2023 ). ### Differences between formal structures and lived practices

The tensions between formal agile frameworks and team practices refer to a well-known problem in organizational research. As already pointed out by Argyris and Schön (1974) the discrepancy between formal structures and lived practices can be understood as a manifestation of the difference between an organization's espoused theories and its theories-in-use. An espoused theory refers to the explicit beliefs, values, and assumptions that organizations claim to follow in their actions. It is what people or organizations say they are doing, or the formal policies and guidelines they assert they are adhering to. This contrasts with theories-in-use, which reflect the actual behaviors and decision-making processes that are observed in practice. A way to explain this discrepancy is offered, for example, by Giddens (1986) structuration theory. He points out that structures and rules of an organization both shape and are shaped by human actions. This process of navigating and modifying formal structures in everyday practices occurs for different reasons. Firstly, formal rules and procedures are not fixed entities; they are dynamic and interpreted by individuals. Secondly, another often found reason is that people often adapt formal rules to fit the practical realities of their work. In the context of the introduction of IT systems, for example, Orlikowski (1992) has shown how users adapted the formal structures of technology implementation to suit their workflows. Finally, Giddens (1986) also emphasizes that formal structures often embody power relations, which affect how they are enacted in practice. Thus, power dynamics shape lived practices, as either those with more power can interpret or bend formal rules to their advantage or those with less power can try to circumvent or reinterpret formal structures to gain power and even reshape the formal structures ( Barley, 1986 ; Barley and Tolbert, 1997 ).

Another major point in this context was the use of the discrepancy to (re)institute control over self-managed teams. As shown in the study of Barker (1993) management can transfer authority to self-managing teams, and thereby creating the appearance of autonomy, while at the same time reinforcing managerial power by letting the employees exercise “concertive control”, i.e. enacting organizational norms through peer-pressure, sometimes more rigid than under direct control of the management. In contrast, for the paradox of team autonomy and organizational control, this could involve raising issues in communities of practice or facilitating more direct dialogue between teams and management ( Moe et al., 2021 ). ### Fostering salience across organizational levels

Building on the discussion of whether paradoxes are latent or salient (see section 2.1 .), especially the argument that paradoxes might be latent for some while salient for others across a hierarchy, a critical task is to ensure their visibility across levels. It is also crucial to recognize that while paradoxes may be visible at different levels, they manifest with varying intensities. In this sense, salience is produced not just by a singular moment of tension, but by its diffusion and persistence over time ( Knight and Paroutis, 2017 ). In these cases, this necessitates communication between these levels about their experiences with paradoxes. The objective is to foster an organizational culture that habituates ambiguity and plurality, promotes the acceptance of diverse perspectives, and avoids the polarization inherent in "us vs. them" mentalities. Specifically, this can be achieved by connecting teams across functions, stimulating cross-hierarchical dialogue, and finding shared understandings ( Berti et al., 2021 ). This approach is also supported by data, as numerous articles emphasize the significance of top management's role ( Hoda and Murugesan, 2016 ; Hodgson and Briand, 2013 ; Lill and Wald, 2021 ; Verwijs and Russo, 2023 ). According to paradox theory, it is vital to acknowledge the different levels within an organization, ensuring not just support but mutual understanding. This understanding must be reciprocal; top management needs to comprehend agile methodologies, and agile teams must understand the broader organizational context, including the perspectives of top management. In fact, one of the articles by Sauer and Nicklich (2021) specifically highlights the importance of addressing all related structures, processes, and roles rather than focusing solely on teams. This aligns closely with paradox theory and our findings, suggesting that agile work necessitates a broader focus beyond the team, encompassing the structures and units surrounding them.
